source_refs.note: Topic 4.3, printed pages 94-95: dehydration synthesis and hydrolysis with the maltose example.

blocks.text: Proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates and lipids are assembled from different kinds of monomers. All these biomolecules join their monomers by the condensation or dehydration process. During condensation an -OH group is removed from one monomer and an -H atom is removed from another monomer. It is also known as dehydration synthesis, because the removal of OH and H means the removal of a water molecule. The formation of maltose from two glucose monomers is an example of a condensation reaction.

blocks.alt: Glucose + Glucose, each drawn as a ring with an OH at both sides; the H of the right OH of the first glucose and the left OH of the second are highlighted. An arrow leads to Maltose: the two rings joined by a bridging O, and a water molecule (H-O-H, highlighted) dropping out below. Labels: Glucose, Glucose, Maltose, Water.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.4: Making of macromolecules (Dehydration synthesis) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.4).

blocks.title: Energy is needed
blocks.text: Energy is required to break chemical bonds when water is extracted from monomers, so cells must supply energy to make macromolecules.

Along with making polymers by combining their monomers, cells keep on breaking polymers too. Hydrolysis is a chemical process in which a macromolecule (polymer) is broken down into smaller fragments by the addition of water molecules. It is the reverse of dehydration synthesis: cells break bonds between monomers by adding water to them. The OH group from a water molecule joins one monomer and the hydrogen joins the second monomer. The breakdown of maltose into two glucose monomers by the addition of a water molecule is an example of hydrolysis.

blocks.alt: Maltose (two rings joined by a bridging O) with a water molecule below whose arrows point at the bridge. An arrow leads to Glucose + Glucose, the added H on the first and the added OH on the second highlighted. Labels: Maltose, Water, Glucose, Glucose.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.5: Breaking of macromolecules (Hydrolysis) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.5).

blocks.title: Why hydrolysis matters
blocks.text: The breakdown of macromolecules is essential in biological processes such as digestion and cellular respiration, where smaller molecules are needed for energy production.
